title: 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash — 10-Year Financials & Earnings Quality
question: Does PCBL turn profit into free cash and earn more than its cost of capital, or did FY2026’s cash strength come from one-time items on a balance sheet that the Aquapharm deal made heavy?

epigraph.quote: “...over the next 30 months, we expect the two companies to have EBITDAs of INR4,000 crores-plus. The acquisition cost is INR3,800 crores.”
epigraph.author: Sanjiv Goenka, Chairman, PCBL conference call on the Aquapharm acquisition, 28 November 2023

web_blocks.html: PCBL’s ten years fall into two regimes. From FY2017 to FY2023 it was a lightly financed carbon black producer. Borrowings stayed between ₹617 Cr and ₹1,029 Cr, and pre-tax return on capital employed ran between 16% and 23% in each year from FY2018 to FY2023. The business converted most earnings into cash [4]. In FY2024 the Aquapharm purchase (about ₹3,850 Cr) and a ₹950 Cr Tamil Nadu greenfield more than doubled capital employed, from ₹3,859 Cr to ₹8,230 Cr. Borrowings rose from ₹1,029 Cr to ₹4,983 Cr [4]. Revenue grew at 11.5% a year from ₹2,470 Cr in FY2015 to ₹8,189 Cr in FY2026. Of the FY2024–FY2026 revenue increase, 68% came from Aquapharm, while carbon black plus power grew 9.2% in two years, from ₹6,181 Cr to ₹6,747 Cr [3][2]. This chapter asks whether the larger balance sheet earns its keep, how good the cash flow really is, and what must change for cash to compound. Every number is audited or drawn from the price-blind Screener feed [4]. TTM and September 2026 columns are interim.

web_blocks.caption: Company EBITDA against Screener operating profit (₹ Cr)
rows: 0.52 net (goodwill impairment 554.72 offset by deferred-tax reversal 554.20)
web_blocks.takeaway: Management quotes the first column. Screener and this chapter’s ratios use the second, because other income is not operating. In FY2026 that other income included ₹10.15 Cr of dividends from group shares and ₹10.01 Cr of investment gains [3][18]. Screener also nets the exceptional item into other income, which is why its FY2026 other income is ₹14 Cr rather than ₹38.59 Cr [4]. Where we quote management’s EBITDA we say so.

web_blocks.caption: PCBL Chemical: annual profit-and-loss history, FY2016–FY2026 and trailing twelve months (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: The TTM column is interim and ends September 2026. Operating margin peaked at 19.4% in FY2021 and fell to 12.7% in FY2023. It recovered to 16.2% and 15.9%, then dropped to 12.7% in FY2026 as interest went from ₹53 Cr in FY2023 to ₹461 Cr in FY2025. Feed EPS of ₹5.03 for FY2026 uses the year-end share count, while audited basic EPS is ₹5.15 on weighted shares [3][4].

web_blocks.html: The margin bridge for FY2026 is a story of squeezed spread and heavier costs. Revenue fell 2.6% to ₹8,189.30 Cr while cost of goods fell only 1.6% (₹5,718.87 Cr), so gross profit dropped ₹124.28 Cr. Employee cost rose 12.2% (₹50.56 Cr) and other expenses rose 14.1% (₹118.97 Cr). That took EBITDA excluding other income down 22.0% to ₹1,042.97 Cr [3]. Within other expenses, miscellaneous items rose 48% to ₹317.15 Cr without itemisation, and outward freight rose 19.4% to ₹206.70 Cr. A net FX gain of ₹75.79 Cr, equal to 7.3% of EBITDA, reduced the line [3]. From there PAT fell 54.4% to ₹198.04 Cr. The fall came from EBITDA (−₹293.81 Cr), other income (−₹8.80 Cr), depreciation (−₹27.08 Cr) and the exceptional charge (−₹24.52 Cr). Lower interest (+₹37.93 Cr) and lower tax (+₹79.65 Cr) cushioned it [3]. Finance cost and the ₹91.82 Cr annual amortisation of Aquapharm intangibles together absorbed 49% of FY2026 EBITDA [3].

web_blocks.caption: PCBL Chemical: balance-sheet history, March 2016 to March 2026 and September 2026 (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: The September 2026 column is interim. Borrowings include lease liabilities in this feed (₹4,989 Cr at March 2026 against ₹4,825.18 Cr of audited borrowings plus ₹163.88 Cr of leases). The jump in other liabilities from ₹2,299 Cr to ₹3,279 Cr in six months is mostly trade payables, examined below [3][4][18].

web_blocks.html: The balance sheet carries a lot of acquired intangibles. Goodwill of ₹606.76 Cr and other intangibles of ₹2,099.27 Cr total ₹2,706.03 Cr, which is 24% of assets and 67% of equity of ₹4,019.15 Cr. Subtracting them leaves tangible equity of ₹1,313 Cr, against net debt (borrowings less cash equivalents) of ₹4,596 Cr [3]. The Aquapharm-related part alone is ₹2,586.7 Cr, or 64% of equity. It comprises goodwill of ₹606.76 Cr, customer intangibles of ₹1,562.72 Cr and product intangibles of ₹417.18 Cr [3]. Debt is mostly floating-rate bank and NBFC loans, with fixed-rate debentures of ₹872.22 Cr. No commercial paper was outstanding at March 2026 [3]. Debentures of ₹487.22 Cr are secured by a first pledge on Aquapharm shares at 1.5 times cover. That is a company-level pledge, not a promoter pledge [3]. Of the ₹4,825 Cr borrowed, ₹2,230 Cr (46%) falls due in FY2028–FY2029. That is the window in which the Andhra Pradesh plant and the battery-materials investments are planned [3][44].

web_blocks.caption: PCBL Chemical: cash-flow history, FY2015–FY2026 (₹ Cr; free cash flow is feed-defined)
web_blocks.takeaway: Across FY2015–FY2026 cash from operations totalled ₹6,538 Cr against reported profit of ₹3,573 Cr, a ratio of 1.8, so conversion is historically good. Over FY2022–FY2026, though, operating cash of ₹4,235 Cr was ₹2,437 Cr short of investing outflows of ₹6,672 Cr. Debt bridged that gap [4]. FY2026’s ₹1,576 Cr is the highest in the series and is examined next.

web_blocks.caption: PCBL Chemical: working-capital days and ROCE, FY2015–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days fell to 62 in FY2026, and the cash conversion cycle fell to 35 days, a 40-day negative working-capital reading on Screener’s basis. ROCE fell from 17–18% (FY2021–FY2023) to 8%. FY2024 and FY2025 days are distorted because the year-end balance sheet included Aquapharm while the income statement did not yet [4][3].

web_blocks.title: The FY2026 cash bridge: what flattered it

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated cash bridge, FY2026 against FY2025 (₹ Cr)
rows: Free cash after interest and leases
Dividends paid / promoter warrant money received
web_blocks.takeaway: FY2026 CFO of ₹1,576 Cr was more than double FY2025’s because working capital swung ₹937 Cr, from absorbing cash to releasing it [3]. Management cites better credit terms with vendors and customers, better inventory management and lower crude [35]. The Integrated Report says “over ₹447 Crores” was released [3]. The cash-flow statement shows ₹529.16 Cr and the balance sheet movement is ₹495 Cr, so three numbers circulate (we use the audited ₹529.16 Cr). Strip the release out and free cash after interest and leases was negative in both years, −₹174 Cr and −₹128 Cr. So FY2026 did not demonstrate self-funding. It demonstrated that a falling-crude year frees working capital. Cash taxes of ₹66.69 Cr were also low, helped by a deferred tax asset of ₹351.96 Cr on unabsorbed depreciation and losses [3].

web_blocks.caption: Debt load and interest coverage
rows: Net debt (borrowings less cash and deposits)
EBITDA excluding other income (Screener operating profit)
Net debt / EBITDA excluding other income
Total debt / LTM company EBITDA (CARE trigger basis; trigger is below 4x)
Borrowings due within one year / in 1–3 years
web_blocks.takeaway: The debt burden rose in FY2026 even though debt fell, because EBITDA fell faster. H1 FY27 coverage improved on a quarter helped by inventory gains and a tariff refund [3][18][4].

web_blocks.html: Three conventions run through this dossier, and every ratio carries its label. “Net debt” is borrowings less cash and deposits, ₹4,696 Cr at September 2026. “LTM company EBITDA” is the company's own EBITDA including other income: H1 FY27 of ₹710 Cr plus H2 FY26 of ₹478.56 Cr, or ₹1,188.56 Cr. Net debt over that is 3.95x at September 2026 and 4.19x at March 2026. Screener's operating profit leaves out other income, so net debt reads 4.09x on ₹1,148 Cr and 4.41x on ₹1,043 Cr. That is a 0.1x to 0.2x gap from the basis alone. Net debt including leases was ₹4,760 Cr at March 2026, or 4.56x on operating profit excluding other income. The Screener TTM figure is the sum of four quarters: Q3 FY26 (₹215 Cr), Q4 FY26 (₹243 Cr), Q1 FY27 (₹396 Cr) and Q2 FY27 (₹294 Cr) [4].

Lenders test total debt, not net debt. CARE's trigger is total debt below 4x PBILDT, and on LTM company EBITDA total debt is 4.15x at September 2026 (₹4,927 Cr over ₹1,188.56 Cr). CARE's own FY2026 reading was 5.02x on its profit measure. That 4.15x is the one test we carry into the re-underwrite triggers in Chapters 0, 5, 7 and 9: total debt below 4 times LTM company EBITDA. It needs EBITDA of about ₹1,232 Cr at today's debt, or about ₹43 Cr more than the last twelve months delivered.

web_blocks.caption: Credit ratings and what the agencies say would change them
rows: AA, Negative (NCD ₹700 Cr, bank facilities ₹800 Cr); commercial paper A1+ [3][52]
The rationale could not be retrieved, so its drivers are not quoted; the date the outlook turned negative was not found
[ICRA]AA, outlook revised to Negative from Stable (stable at 17 Mar 2025) [44][42]

Pressure on profitability “likely to persist over the next few quarters” and weak Aquapharm performance; downgrade on “inability to improve the profitability from current level on a sustained basis” or delay in correcting total debt/OPBDITA [44]
CARE AA, Negative, A1+; outlook revised from Stable (18 Sep 2025) [46][43]
“Inability to improve TD/PBILDT to below 4x on a sustained basis”; total debt/PBILDT was 5.02x in FY2026 against 5.07x in FY2024 [46]
web_blocks.takeaway: All three agencies sit at AA with a negative outlook. The two that publish triggers tie them to the same two items: profitability and total debt relative to EBITDA, with CARE naming 4x. On September 2026 total debt of ₹4,927 Cr, that needs EBITDA of about ₹1,232 Cr against LTM company EBITDA of ₹1,188.56 Cr (₹1,148 Cr excluding other income). CARE records liquidity as strong and expects planned capex to delay improvement in the capital structure [46].

web_blocks.caption: Quarterly results, Q2 FY24 to Q2 FY27 (₹ Cr; company EBITDA includes other income)
rows: Aquapharm closes 31 Jan 2024; interest steps up
Goodwill impairment and deferred-tax reversal net about nil
Volume up 8.8% year on year, EBITDA down 25%
₹21 Cr Labour Codes charge not tax-effected, so tax was 80% of reported PBT
About ₹70 Cr low-cost inventory gain; ₹40–50 Cr expected to reverse
₹33 Cr US tariff refund; other income ₹16 Cr
web_blocks.takeaway: The December 2025 quarter’s ₹2 Cr profit and 80% tax rate was an accounting event layered on real weakness. The ₹21 Cr exceptional charge was not tax-effected in the quarter (tax of ₹8 Cr on pre-exceptional PBT of ₹31 Cr is 26%). Even so, PBT before the exceptional item had already fallen to ₹31 Cr from ₹124 Cr a year earlier, on EBITDA per tonne of ₹13,800 [35][13]. H1 FY27 EBITDA of ₹710 Cr is up 18% on ₹603 Cr. Removing about ₹70 Cr of inventory gain and ₹33 Cr of tariff refund leaves about ₹607 Cr, flat on last year. Ex other income it is ₹587 Cr against ₹585 Cr (our estimates from management’s figures) [39][40][18]. Sources: [4][5][7][8][9][10][12][13][15][16][18].

web_blocks.title: Dividend against earnings and free cash

web_blocks.caption: Dividend, earnings and free cash (₹ Cr)
rows: Free cash after interest and leases
Free cash after interest and leases, before working capital
web_blocks.takeaway: Management says the normal payout is 40–50% of profit. On 3 February 2026 the CFO said “the board has decided not to reduce dividend payout for now”, and the investor-relations head said that on a normalised level payout “would still be 45-50%” [35]. In FY2026 the cash dividend was 114% of consolidated PAT (96% of standalone PAT). It was funded by the working-capital release and ₹336 Cr of promoter warrant money, of which ₹116.42 Cr, or 35%, went back to the promoter group as dividend [3]. Net borrowings still fell ₹454 Cr [36]. The dividend has not been covered by free cash before working-capital swings in FY2025 or FY2026, and the H1 FY27 coverage depends on one-offs.

web_blocks.title: Return on capital against an explicit cost of capital

web_blocks.caption: ROCE decomposition, FY2022 to FY2026 (EBIT = pre-exceptional PBT plus interest, including other income)
rows: Capital employed, year end (equity + reserves + borrowings incl. leases, ₹ Cr)
Post-tax return at 25% tax, year-end capital
web_blocks.takeaway: From FY2023 to FY2026 capital employed rose by ₹5,136 Cr while EBIT rose by ₹74 Cr, an incremental pre-tax return of 1.4%. Counted at EBITDA excluding other income (+₹312 Cr) it is 6.1%, still below the 7.8% cost of debt. FY2024’s average-capital figure is flattered because the acquisition closed in the final quarter. Our assumptions for the hurdle are a pre-tax cost of debt of 7.8% (audited), a cost of equity of 13% (our assumption, not a sourced figure), 25% tax, and book-value weights of 45% equity and 55% debt. Together they give a WACC of about 9%. We use 10% post-tax to allow for execution risk. The company’s own post-tax discount rate for the Aquapharm cash-generating unit is 13.70% [3]. At 10%, FY2026 capital of ₹8,995 Cr needs EBIT of about ₹1,199 Cr (a 13.3% pre-tax return), against ₹709 Cr. The post-tax return was below even 9% in every year since FY2024, including the FY2025 peak (8.4%).

web_blocks.caption: Aquapharm: acquisition case against delivery
rows: ₹3,800 Cr headline; consideration ₹3,850 Cr; cash outflow ₹3,708 Cr in FY2024 [27][2][5]
Funded mainly with debt, which has not fallen: borrowings including leases were ₹4,983 Cr at March 2024 and ₹5,083 Cr at September 2026 [4][3]
Chairman: FY2024 projected ₹370 Cr on revenue of ₹2,045 Cr, a 20% margin [27]; CFO, 23 May 2024: “on a full year basis is going to add another 250 to 300 crore” [28]
5.0% (FY2025), 4.2% (FY2026), 4.6% annualised H1 FY27; break-even to the cost of debt would need ₹300 Cr, before depreciation
Chemicals PBIT ₹17.43 Cr on segment assets of ₹4,226.04 Cr = 0.4% (FY2025 1.5%); adding back ₹91.82 Cr purchase-price amortisation, 2.6% [3]
FY2025: goodwill impaired ₹554.72 Cr, offset by a ₹554.20 Cr deferred-tax reversal; forecast EBITDA margin 21–24%, discount rate 18.50% [3]
FY2026 test passed with margin assumed at 16–20% and discount rate 13.70%; actual margin 11.2% is below both ranges [3]
Aquapharm’s share of group profit was −₹68.70 Cr in FY2026 (−₹29.14 Cr in FY2025) while it holds 68.7% of consolidated net assets (₹2,760.08 Cr) [3]
CFO: “a good potential for some 500-600 crore kind of tax savings” [28]
Deferred tax asset on unabsorbed depreciation and losses ₹351.96 Cr (FY2025 ₹229.46 Cr); real but realised only with taxable profit [3]
web_blocks.takeaway: On the evidence to November 2026 the acquisition has not earned its cost of capital. EBITDA of ₹162 Cr is about 65% of the bottom of the CFO’s own range (₹250 Cr). The earnings return on price paid is below the cost of the debt used, and the impairment model assumes margins the business has not reached. The mitigants are real: sequential recovery to ₹47 Cr and ₹42 Cr of EBITDA in Q1 and Q2 FY27, home-care volume growth and the DGTR anti-dumping recommendation on HEDP and ATMP. None is yet in the numbers [18][40][56]. Chapter 5 audits the promises against delivery.

web_blocks.title: Related parties and the investment book

web_blocks.caption: Related-party and group-investment items (₹ Cr, consolidated)
rows: CESC ₹253.22 Cr plus other listed and unlisted holdings; dividend income ₹10.15 Cr, a 2.2% yield on cost against 7.8% debt cost, so about ₹26 Cr a year of negative carry if the capital retired debt [3]
Fair-value change on those holdings (through OCI)
55.6% of consolidated power sales; terms said to be arm’s-length [3]
Up 24%; counterparty not named in the note [3]
1.6 Cr shares at ₹280, ₹448 Cr in total; promoter stake 51.41% to 53.38% [3]
web_blocks.takeaway: Nothing here is hidden. The transactions are disclosed, the statutory auditor’s opinion is unmodified and the Board report records no material related-party transactions [3]. The point is capital allocation. About 4% of assets and 11.5% of equity sit in group shares that earn a fraction of the cost of debt, while net debt is ₹4,596 Cr. Over half of power revenue and of dividends flows to or from the controlling group. Promoter pledge is nil per the aggregator and broker data we could read [72][65]. The exchange’s September 2026 pattern is an image file we could not machine-read [53].

web_blocks.title: The September 2026 inventory and payables jump

web_blocks.caption: Trade working capital, September 2025 to September 2026 (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: H1 FY27 working capital absorbed ₹219 Cr, CFO was ₹363 Cr and capex ₹202 Cr [18]. What management said: nothing on this balance-sheet jump directly. The CFO said crude “moved back to $100 and beyond. As we speak, it is $110. And consequently, we didn't see inventory buildup” at customers. Aquapharm’s CEO said “we have expanded our critical raw material inventory coverage”, with a balance between “supply security and optimal working capital efficiency” [40]. On 30 April 2026 the CFO had guided only “another INR100 crores worth of incremental working capital” at $90 crude [36]. What we infer: Brent averaged $97 in Q1 FY27 against $78 in Q4 FY26. March inventory was carried at costs set when Brent was around $60–65 in early 2026, so price explains a large part. Payables rose almost one-for-one with inventories, so net funding was ₹170 Cr [39][40]. Price alone, though (crude at $97–110 against $65 is 49–69% higher), does not explain +93%. So some of it is more physical stock, deliberately, and the company does not publish tonnes held. Net: FY2026’s ₹529 Cr release and H1 FY27’s ₹219 Cr absorption are largely one crude-price round trip. The higher payables raise dependence on supplier and bank credit while ratings are on negative outlook.

web_blocks.takeaway: The reporting is clean and conservative on receivables and contingencies. The weak spots are judgments, not irregularities: the goodwill test, the unitemised ₹317 Cr miscellaneous expense line, and the covenant deferment.

web_blocks.html: Reported earnings are accurate but low in quality for three reasons. First, FY2026 profit was depressed by a spread squeeze, and FY2026 cash was inflated by a one-time working-capital release. Neither describes a steady state. Second, H1 FY27’s 18% EBITDA growth is about flat once the inventory gain and tariff refund are removed. Third, about half of EBITDA goes to interest and acquisition amortisation. Against that, receivables are clean and the audit is unmodified. Pre-working-capital operating cash flow of ₹1,114 Cr in FY2026 is real. The carbon black franchise earned 16–23% pre-tax returns on a lighter balance sheet for six years. We put the odds at roughly two to one that the core franchise can earn its cost of capital in a normal spread year. The capital deployed since FY2024 has so far earned less than the debt that funded it.

Illustration: TTM EBITDA ₹1,148 Cr less annualised interest ₹392 Cr, leases ₹50 Cr, FY2026-level cash tax ₹67 Cr and the ₹300 Cr FY2027 capex guide leaves about ₹339 Cr before working capital, against dividends of ₹177 Cr already paid in H1 FY27 (₹226 Cr in FY2026); the ₹2,230 Cr due in FY2028–FY2029 must come from elsewhere [39]
About ₹300 Cr EBITDA just to match the cost of debt on the price; margin 16–20% as the impairment test assumes
Quarterly EBITDA moving to the ₹75 Cr run-rate management has cited [36], and the anti-dumping duty notified

Net trade working capital held near ₹1,100–1,150 Cr
Dividend ₹177 Cr in H1; Andhra Phase I about ₹1,100 Cr planned [3]

web_blocks.takeaway: Cash compounding is credible only if EBITDA moves about a third above its trailing level while capital stays flat, or if Aquapharm earns its assumed margins. Neither is visible yet. The evidence therefore supports a profitable cyclical franchise with a stretched balance sheet and no demonstrated compounding.

web_blocks.title: Price-blind business-level conclusion
paragraphs: Business quality: cyclical and conditional. The carbon black core is the largest domestic producer, converts earnings into cash historically and earned 16–23% pre-tax returns before FY2024. The consolidated business since FY2024 earns below its cost of capital and funds its dividend with working-capital swings and promoter equity. It also carries net debt of 4.1–4.4 times operating profit excluding other income (3.95–4.2 times company EBITDA) with three negative-outlook credit ratings.

KPI health: pass with watch. Volume, specialty mix, power and receivables are healthy. EBITDA per tonne, utilisation, Aquapharm profit and net-debt reduction are the failing indicators. The guidance on several has been lowered or deferred (Chapter 5).

web_blocks.html: What would change our mind is a combination of three signals. The first is a sustained EBITDA per tonne of ₹20,000 or more without inventory gains and with volumes recovering. The second is quarterly Aquapharm EBITDA above ₹75 Cr. The third is total debt falling below 4 times LTM company EBITDA (4.15x at September 2026, CARE's own trigger basis) while dividends are covered by free cash before working capital. The opposite signals are a further covenant deferment, a goodwill impairment, or a payables-to-inventory unwind that costs cash.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a confession about how I read a company like PCBL. I do not begin with the profit; I begin with the question of what the cash did. Profit is an opinion, as the old accountants say, and cash is a fact. So I pulled out the ten-year record, and before we look at any single year I want you to see its shape. For six years, from FY2018 to FY2023, this was a lean carbon black producer. Its debt never went above about ₹1,000 Cr, and it earned between 16 and 23 per cent a year before tax on the money invested. Then, in a single year, two decisions changed it: a ₹3,850 Cr purchase of Aquapharm and a ₹950 Cr new plant in Tamil Nadu. Capital employed more than doubled, to ₹8,230 Cr, and so did debt.

Hold that moment in your mind, because the Chairman gave it a clock. On 28 November 2023, announcing the deal, Sanjiv Goenka said that “over the next 30 months, we expect the two companies to have EBITDAs of INR4,000 crores-plus. The acquisition cost is INR3,800 crores.” He added, “I am personally very debt averse.” Now, let us compare that with what happened. The company’s EBITDA for the twenty-seven months from January 2024 to March 2026 was ₹2,798 Cr, which is 78 per cent of the pro-rated promise, and the borrowings on the balance sheet were ₹4,983 Cr in March 2024 and ₹5,083 Cr in September 2026. I am not accusing anyone of bad faith. I am telling you that the deal case has not yet shown up in the cash.

Next, the profit and loss. In FY2026 revenue slipped 2.6 per cent to ₹8,189 Cr, and EBITDA excluding other income fell 22 per cent to ₹1,043 Cr. A word on that definition, because you will meet two numbers in the market. The company quotes EBITDA of ₹1,082 Cr, which includes ₹39 Cr of other income, and the data aggregators quote ₹1,043 Cr, which does not. I show leverage on both bases, because other income, here mostly dividends on group shares and investment gains, is not operating and moves the ratio by 0.1 to 0.2 times. Below the EBITDA line the damage compounds: interest of ₹423 Cr and depreciation of ₹373 Cr, a quarter of which is the amortisation of Aquapharm’s purchase price, left profit after tax at ₹198 Cr, down 54 per cent.

Then comes the line that surprises people: operating cash flow of ₹1,576 Cr, almost eight times profit and the highest in the twelve-year series. Let us walk through how that happened. Receivables fell by ₹428 Cr, inventories fell by ₹259 Cr, and the net effect of working capital was a release of ₹529 Cr, compared with an absorption of ₹408 Cr the year before. The CFO, on 3 February 2026, put it this way: it came “partly because of our being able to negotiate better credit terms with our vendors and our customers and better inventory management,” and “also because crude came down in this period.” Notice that the second reason is not a management action. It is the oil price, and the oil price does not do favours twice.

Strip the release out, and the picture changes. Free cash after capex, interest and leases was ₹355 Cr in FY2026, but without the working-capital release it was minus ₹174 Cr. The year before it was minus ₹128 Cr on the same basis. In both years the business did not generate enough cash to pay for its capital spending and its interest bill, before it paid a rupee of dividend. That is not a verdict on the franchise; it is a measure of how heavy the balance sheet has become, with interest and acquisition amortisation together absorbing about half of EBITDA.

Now to the dividend, because it is where the cash story meets the shareholder. The company paid ₹6 a share in FY2026, ₹226 Cr, which was 114 per cent of consolidated profit. When an analyst asked on 3 February 2026 whether the company had gone overboard, the CFO answered: “the visibility around performance and cash flow remains very strong. And therefore, the board has decided not to reduce dividend payout for now.” Management’s stated norm is 40 to 50 per cent. I see two things here. First, the payout was funded by the working-capital release and by ₹336 Cr of promoter money received through warrants; ₹116 Cr of the dividend went straight back to the promoter group. Second, in the first half of FY27 the company paid another ₹177 Cr while its free cash after interest and leases was minus ₹23 Cr, because working capital absorbed ₹219 Cr.

Let me now show you how the lenders see this balance sheet, because they have more to lose than we do. Goodwill and acquired intangibles of ₹2,706 Cr make up two-thirds of equity, so the tangible equity is only about ₹1,313 Cr against net debt of ₹4,596 Cr. Of the ₹4,825 Cr borrowed, ₹2,230 Cr falls due in FY2028 and FY2029, exactly when the Andhra Pradesh plant and the battery-materials spending are meant to arrive. Interest cover on operating profit after depreciation was 1.58 times in FY2026, and net debt was 4.4 times operating profit excluding other income (4.2 times the company's own EBITDA). The lenders' own test is total debt, which is 4.15 times trailing company EBITDA against CARE's trigger of 4 times. ICRA, on 12 February 2026, said the pressure on profitability was “likely to persist over the next few quarters” and moved its outlook to negative; CARE followed on 7 July 2026 and said it would restore a stable outlook “upon meaningful improvement in its operating profitability.” CRISIL’s AA carries a negative outlook as well. None of them is saying the company is in trouble. They are saying that the room for error has gone.

Which brings us to the September 2026 balance sheet, where I want to be careful to separate what we know from what I am inferring. Inventories rose from ₹1,024 Cr to ₹1,981 Cr in six months, and trade payables rose almost one-for-one, from ₹1,447 Cr to ₹2,428 Cr. Management did not address this directly. The CFO said crude had gone back to $110 and customers had destocked, and Aquapharm’s CEO said the company had “expanded our critical raw material inventory coverage.” On 30 April the CFO had guided to only about ₹100 Cr of extra working capital. My reading is that most of it is price, because crude moved from about $65 to the $97 to $110 range, but price alone cannot explain a 93 per cent rise. Some is deliberate stock. Net funding need was only ₹170 Cr. The lesson is simple: the ₹529 Cr release and the ₹219 Cr absorption are one crude-price round trip, not a change in earning power.

One more detail from the quarterly record will save you from a common trap. In the December 2025 quarter profit after tax was ₹2 Cr and the tax rate was 80 per cent, and a hurried reader might think a tax problem or a collapse. It was neither. The company took a ₹21 Cr one-time charge for the new Labour Codes and did not claim tax relief on it in that quarter, so tax of ₹8 Cr landed on pre-tax profit of only ₹10 Cr. The real weakness sat higher up: profit before that charge was ₹31 Cr, against ₹124 Cr a year earlier, because carbon black earned only ₹13,800 a tonne. I mention it because accounting noise can hide an operating message, and it can also manufacture a fake one. You and I should always ask which it is.

What about the earnings in H1 FY27, which look so much better? EBITDA of ₹710 Cr is 18 per cent above last year. But in Q1 the CFO told investors, “we did about close to INR70-odd crores” of low-cost-inventory gain, and “This quarter we have some extraordinary benefit of low-cost inventory, which is unlikely to be repeated.” In Q2 there was a ₹33 Cr refund of US tariffs, or ₹2,300 a tonne. Take both out and H1 EBITDA is about ₹607 Cr against ₹603 Cr a year ago. That is flat. I would not call it weak, given that volume fell 17 per cent in Q2 by choice. I would call it a company that is holding its profit steady while the headline improves.

Let me now turn to the Aquapharm return check, because the capital allocation of the last three years stands or falls on it. The CFO said on 23 May 2024 that Aquapharm “on a full year basis is going to add another 250 to 300 crore.” The actual figures are ₹194 Cr in FY2025 and ₹162 Cr in FY2026. On ₹3,850 Cr paid, that is a 4.2 per cent EBITDA return, before depreciation and tax, against a cost of debt of 7.8 per cent. The segment earned ₹17 Cr of pre-tax profit on ₹4,226 Cr of assets. And the impairment test that keeps goodwill intact assumes margins of 16 to 20 per cent, while the actual margin is 11.2. There is good news at the margin, with EBITDA of ₹47 Cr and ₹42 Cr in the last two quarters and a recommended anti-dumping duty, but you and I should wait for it to show in the numbers.

Now, what return do we actually need, and what would it take? I have to make an assumption here and I want you to see it: I take a cost of equity of 13 per cent, which is my assumption and not a published figure, a cost of debt of 7.8 per cent from the audited accounts and a 25 per cent tax rate. That gives a WACC of about 9 per cent, and I use 10 per cent as the hurdle. On ₹8,995 Cr of capital that requires EBIT of about ₹1,200 Cr, against ₹709 Cr in FY2026 and ₹1,038 Cr even at the FY2025 peak. In other words, a repeat of the best year would still not earn the hurdle on today’s balance sheet. Between FY2023 and FY2026 capital employed grew by ₹5,136 Cr and EBIT by ₹74 Cr.

Is the governance a problem? I do not think so, and I want to be fair. The auditor’s opinion is unmodified, receivables are clean, contingent liabilities are small, and no promoter shares are pledged on the data we could read. What I notice instead is capital allocation: ₹464 Cr sits in shares of group companies that earned ₹10 Cr in dividends while the company pays 7.8 per cent on its debt; over half of power sales go to group utilities; and the one judgment on which the whole acquisition rests, the goodwill test, passes only because the discount rate was cut by 480 basis points.

So where does that leave you as an owner? My judgment is that this is a profitable, cyclical business with a franchise worth having, a stretched balance sheet and no demonstrated compounding of cash. The credit agencies, all three at AA with a negative outlook, say much the same in their own language. For compounding to become credible you would need to see EBITDA about a third above its trailing level, or Aquapharm earning the margins its own impairment model assumes, with total debt below four times LTM company EBITDA (4.15 times in September 2026) and dividends covered by free cash before working-capital swings. Until then, treat each strong cash quarter as a question: is it earnings power or is it the oil price? That is the discipline the rest of the dossier will apply.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A promise with a clock attached is the most useful thing a manager can give an analyst, because the clock does the auditing. Thirty months were promised for the deal to pay for itself; nearly three years in, gross debt is where it started and the cash that did arrive in FY2026 came from falling crude and promoter equity. The lesson is not to distrust the people but to measure the claim against the cash, and to keep a separate column for the cash that nobody will be able to repeat.

book_callouts.title: THE TWO-QUESTION CASH TEST
book_callouts.text: For any strong cash year, ask two questions. Would free cash after interest, leases and capex still be positive without the working-capital change? And did the dividend and any capital raised come from that free cash or from something else? PCBL’s FY2025 and FY2026 both fail the first test and its dividend fails the second.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hurdle I set, 10 per cent after tax, is deliberately modest next to the company’s own 13.7 per cent for Aquapharm. Even so, the FY2025 peak year does not reach it on today’s capital. That is the real measure of what the last three years cost: not one bad quarter, but a base that now needs a much better business to justify itself.
